title: The thread and the king
hookLine: Lakshmi ties a thread on a king's wrist to bring Vishnu home; why the rakhi prayer names King Bali
carry: a rakhi binds a promise you keep
last: MAHA SHIVARATRI: A SIGN OF THE ENDLESS LIGHT.

lines: A KING WHO NEVER SAID NO.
cards: There was once a king named Bali, an asura king, and he never said no to anyone who asked him for anything. That habit cost him his whole kingdom; on day one hundred fifty-four you'll hear how.
He ended up ruling a world below this one, and Vishnu, moved by his goodness, promised to stand guard at his door. Which left Vishnu's wife, the goddess Lakshmi, alone at home.
So one full moon, many families say, she goes down to Bali's palace in disguise, with a thread in her hand.

teach.h: LAKSHMI TIES, BALI KEEPS HIS WORD.
teach.b: She ties the thread on Bali's wrist and calls him brother. A sister! Ask for anything.
And Lakshmi asks for the one thing she came for: the guard at your door. Bali, who has never broken his word, lets Vishnu go home.
It's a story many families tell for Raksha Bandhan, and though it isn't in the oldest texts, it echoes in the prayer.

When the thread is tied, many priests and some families say a short Sanskrit verse that begins yena baddho bali raja. Its sense: with the thread that bound mighty King Bali, I bind you; hold fast, don't slip. Bound how?
The old story says Vamana had him tied with Varuna's ropes, but many teachers read the real bond as his word: Bali never broke it. That's the teaching under the rakhi.
Raksha means protection, bandhan a bond, and the thread is a promise made before God.
In Hindu teaching, keeping your word is part of dharma, the right way to live, and Bali is a model of it: he kept his promises even when they cost him everything.
In many homes, the sister circles a small lamp before her brother's face, puts a red tilak on his forehead, ties the thread on his right wrist, and feeds him a sweet.
He gives a gift and a promise to protect her. Today rakhis are tied between sisters, cousins and close friends too. And today: a rakhi isn't a bracelet.
It's a promise you can see on your wrist all week, and it asks Bali's question: will you keep it when it costs you something?

how: On the full moon of Shravan, many Hindu sisters perform a small arti for their brothers, apply a tilak, tie a rakhi on the wrist while a short verse naming King Bali may be said, and feed them a sweet; brothers give a gift and a promise of protection, and today rakhis are also tied between sisters, cousins and friends.

o: a lucky charm sewn into a baby's pillow
a wedding thread tied by the bride's father
a bond of protection, tied as a thread on the wrist

games.q: the thread and the king — tap the pairs.
p: the king who never broke his word
tied a thread to bring Vishnu home

s: the rakhi verse names King Bali
yena baddho bali raja: with the thread that bound King Bali, I bind you.
the Lakshmi-and-Bali story comes from the oldest Vedic texts
it's a later, popular telling. the verse naming Bali is older, and Vishnu guarding his door is in the Puranas.
rakhis are tied only by sisters on brothers
sisters, cousins and close friends tie them too.

games.q: you're King Bali. Lakshmi has tied a thread on your wrist, and she asks for the guard at your door: Vishnu himself. what do you do?
o: keep your word and let him go home.
games.why: Bali never breaks his word, even when it costs him. that's why, many say, the rakhi verse names him.

practice: Think of one promise you've made to someone, out loud or not: to show up, to look out for them, to call. If you have a thread, tie it on your wrist; if not, just rest your fingers where a rakhi would go.
If you pray, say the name you pray to. Then make the promise again, silently, once, and hold your wrist for a few breaths. Then let your hand go.

wordCard.voice: Raksha Bandhan. The bond of protection: a thread tied on the full moon of Shravan, with a promise that holds.

orig.note: Sanskrit: raksha, protection, and bandhana, a tie or bond.

carryVoice: Your line: a rakhi binds a promise you keep. Bound like Bali, by his word. One hundred fifty days now.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 8.22–8.23 (Bali sent to Sutala; Vishnu promises to guard his door)
Bhavishya Purana, Uttara Parva (the raksha rite and the verse 'yena baddho bali raja')
